name: Serve & Give
tagline: Eyes that see the need and hands that move toward it — time, money, presence, and effort given gladly. Prerequisites here are suggestions; character grows in a spiral.

skills.name: See who needs help
skills.gotItWhen: You spot the need before anyone points it out — the person carrying too much, the kid on the edge of the group, the job nobody's gotten to — because your eyes have gotten in the habit of sweeping the room for somebody besides you.
looksLike: The teacher is juggling a box, a laptop, and a coffee, and you're holding the door before she asks.
You clock the kid sitting alone at lunch — whoever else doesn't.
Walking home, you notice the neighbor's yard is buried in leaves and file it away as something you could do.
waysToBuild: Play the quiet game everywhere you go for a week: 'who in this room could use a hand right now?'
Trade at dinner: 'who did you notice today?' — noticing counts even before doing.
Walk your own street once with fresh eyes and list three needs you'd never spotted before.

skills.name: Help without being asked
skills.gotItWhen: At home, when you see the need, you move toward it — the dishes get done, the crying sibling gets scooped up, the groceries come in from the car — before anyone asks, because being asked was never the point.
looksLike: The dishwasher is clean and full, so you empty it — simply because you're the one standing there.
A little sibling is melting down while dinner's being cooked, and you're the one who swoops in.
The car pulls in from the grocery run and you're already at the trunk.
waysToBuild: Pick one daily window — right after school, right before dinner — and hunt for one unasked help in it.
Run a private streak: one unasked help a day for two weeks, no announcing.
Watch what a parent always ends up doing, and quietly take one of those jobs over.

skills.name: Give some of what you have
skills.gotItWhen: Some of what's yours — money, things, treats — regularly goes to someone else, given gladly and by your own choice, at a size that actually costs you something.
looksLike: You split the treat and hand over the bigger half without ceremony.
Something you've outgrown but still like goes to a kid who'd love it — not to the top shelf of your closet.
There's real money in your giving envelope, from your own pocket, and you're the one who put it there.
waysToBuild: When money comes in (allowance, gifts, jobs — see Money & Work's earning skills), decide the give-portion before you spend anything.
Once a season, give away one thing you still actually like — and notice what that feels like versus giving leftovers.
Pick one cause or person you genuinely care about, so your giving has a face.

skills.name: Show up for people
skills.gotItWhen: When it matters to someone you care about — the recital, the hospital room, the worst week of their year — you're there on purpose, because you've learned that presence is a gift only you can give.
looksLike: Your sibling's concert has you in the audience — no dragging required.
A friend's grandparent dies; you don't know what to say, and you go anyway.
A teammate is out for the season, and you're still checking in after everyone else has moved on.
waysToBuild: Say yes to the next three invitations that feel skippable, and notice what your being there did.
When someone's hurting and you have no words, go anyway — 'I'm here' is a complete sentence.
Keep other people's big days on your own calendar, so showing up is planned, not lucky.

skills.name: Serve where no one sees
skills.gotItWhen: Some of your serving happens where nobody will ever know it was you — done quietly, credit never collected — and the doing itself has become the whole reward.
looksLike: A sibling's dreaded chore is mysteriously already done, and you let the mystery stand.
You clean up a mess nobody saw you near, and dinner passes without you mentioning it.
Someone else gets thanked for a thing you did — and you let them keep it.
waysToBuild: Do one secret act of service a week for a month; if you get caught, shrug and change the subject.
Notice the itch to be credited when it comes — outlasting that itch is the actual training.
Find a job that's invisible by nature (the mud on the cleats, the crumbs under the toaster) and own it silently.

skills.name: Take the job nobody wants
skills.gotItWhen: When the worst job in the room is up for grabs — the trash bag, the crying toddler, the cleanup after everyone drifts off — you're the one who volunteers, and you do it with genuine cheer, like it's a privilege someone had to win.
looksLike: The party is winding down and you're bagging trash while everyone else says long goodbyes.
The carpool toddler is screaming, and you climb into the back seat next to the car seat.
The group project's boring job sits unclaimed until you take it — and then it's done well.
waysToBuild: At the next family event, find the worst job and claim it before anyone has to ask.
Do it cheerfully enough that nobody feels they owe you — the cheer is half the gift.
Trade stories at dinner about the worst jobs anyone took that week, and let them be funny instead of noble.

skills.name: Serve alongside others
skills.gotItWhen: You can join an organized effort — a food bank shift, a church workday, a mission team — take direction from whoever's running it, pull your real weight from start time through cleanup, and be someone the organizers hope comes back.
looksLike: At the food bank you're still boxing cans at the end, when the first-hour energy is long gone.
Your task finishes and you find the leader to ask 'what's next?' instead of drifting to your phone.
The workday organizer greets you by name — because you're the kid who finishes things.
waysToBuild: Sign up for one real shift — food bank, park cleanup, church workday — and stay through the un-fun ending.
Ask the person in charge which job nobody wants, and take that one.
Bring a friend next time and show them the ropes — pulling others in is part of pulling your weight.

skills.name: Speak up for someone
skills.gotItWhen: When someone is being left out, mocked, or talked over, you can put your voice on their side — the left-out kid gets your invitation, the pile-on stops at your message, the unheard idea gets repeated with their name on it — even when it costs you a little standing.
looksLike: There's a new kid eating alone, and 'come sit with us' is your line.
The group chat turns on someone, and your message is the one that breaks the pile-on instead of joining it.
The quiet kid's idea gets steamrolled, and you say 'wait — go back to what she said,' with her name attached.
waysToBuild: Decide your lines before you need them — an invitation line, a pile-on-breaker — so they're loaded when it counts.
Practice the credit relay: restate a steamrolled idea with the person's name until it's a reflex.
After a real moment, debrief it with a parent: what it cost you, and what it bought them.

skills.name: Look after littler ones
skills.gotItWhen: Younger kids are safe with you and glad to see you — you get down on their level, keep them out of harm's way, keep it genuinely fun, and hand them back happier than you found them; you're the big kid the little ones hope shows up.
looksLike: At the family gathering, you've got the toddler cousins running a game so the adults can actually talk.
A shy little kid is frozen at the edge of the party, and you're the one who folds them in.
The neighborhood littles spot you at the park and light up.
waysToBuild: Own a regular slot with a younger sibling or cousin — bath time, book time, the after-dinner wiggles hour.
Learn five games that need zero equipment, so you're never the big kid standing around.
Take a babysitting course, or apprentice as a mother's helper while a parent is still in the house.

skills.name: Serve people not like you
skills.gotItWhen: You've served people whose lives are genuinely unlike yours — a different age, ability, language, neighborhood, or need — with respect instead of pity, learning their names and their stories, and you've let the experience actually change how you see them and yourself.
looksLike: At the nursing home you know the residents' names and stories — not just the visit schedule.
You serve alongside people who don't share your language, and you find ways to work and laugh together anyway.
At the shelter you slow down and talk with someone, and come home thinking about a person, not a project.
waysToBuild: Pick one service opportunity that honestly stretches you — through church, school, or a local organization — and go more than once.
Make learning names your first job at any new place; everything real starts there.
Debrief afterward with someone you trust: what surprised you, what was uncomfortable, what changed?

skills.name: Give your time regularly
skills.gotItWhen: One cause or person gets your time on a rhythm — steady, scheduled, real — across a whole season, and you keep showing up after the shine wears off, because by now they're counting on you.
looksLike: The Sunday kids' room roster has your name on it, and most weeks it has you in it.
Deep into the season it's a lot less exciting than week one — and you're still there.
When you truly can't make it, you arrange your own coverage instead of just not appearing.
waysToBuild: Pick one commitment sized honestly — a month, a semester — and put it in your calendar like school.
Expect the week the shine wears off (it's usually around week three) and decide now that you'll show up through it.
At the end of the season, decide on purpose: renew, resize, or hand it off well.

skills.name: Own a corner of the world
skills.gotItWhen: Some person, place, or cause is simply yours now — nobody assigned it, nobody backs you up on it, and everyone around it has learned they can count on you: the walk gets shoveled, the kid gets mentored, the shelf gets stocked, because you exist and you decided.
looksLike: First snow falls, and the elderly neighbor's walk is clear before school — no arrangement, no reminder; it's just what happens now.
A younger kid at church or school is your kid to encourage, and you track their games and their hard weeks like they matter — because they do.
If you moved away, something in your corner of the world would quietly go undone until somebody noticed the hole you left.
waysToBuild: Look back at what noticing, hidden service, and your regular commitment have been pointing at — a corner is probably already choosing you.
Claim it quietly; no announcement required, and none wanted.
Keep it through at least one full season — through the boring stretch — before you even think about adding another.
